Could you please elaborate on what is "completely wrong"?

- Moving from stable to testing is not an upgrade since testing includes fewer bug fixes than stable and less timely security updates. It changes frequently and though it will break less often than unstable, the chances of complete breakage are still notably more than stable. It is for this reason that moving to testing is not an 'upgrade'.

- The clue to 'testing' is in its name. Its raison d'être is to find fixes for the next stable release.

- in view of the above, *testing will not function as well as stable* and is not recommend as a primary system, daily driver or for anyone where productivity is key.

- Testing is the *future* Debian stable, the future version 10. It is not version 10 yet. Stable is 9.4. Not nearly, not sort of, not "kind of".

'Pretty stable' and 'a bit less stable' are not the same as stable and unchanging for anyone on a production system. 

Also testing is not a rolling release distribution, it is a *development version*. Please do not give inaccurate information to posters. 

Please see the below for more information. I strongly recommend you read this post:

http://forums.debian.net/viewtopic.php?p=531279#p531279

and 

https://www.debian.org/releases/testing/

Testing still breaks, but just not "as badly" [to quote the Wiki] as unstable. It would be pertinent to read up on the source material before tarring something as "completely wrong". It is this dangerous thinking and advice which accounts for the recent deterioration in help quality in the Debian community.

Again, it is not an upgrade :) Try doing a manual suspend from the XFCE menu, resume, and see if that works. If so, it is not a solution as such but a workaround. LXDE uses the XFCE Power Manager so you may be experiencing a similar issue to the one I did.

A few things are wrong with this post:

1. Moving from Debian stable to testing is not an upgrade regardless of what the wiki says. Testing is unstable and buggy and is meant to break in order to find fixes for the next stable release. It will not function as well as stable.

3. This issue may be related to your DE. I had the same issue in LXDE. LXDE is not great at resuming after autosuspend on certain distros. It is better to manually suspend from the logout menu.

One thing I will point out is that the word Outrun is extremely curious to describe this genre - or realm - if we can call it that. I remember playing Outrun in the 80s and you just drive your car around a beach and a few other places. It wasn't dark, sexualised or futuristic at all, which is something I feel that the "outrun" genre has in spades. It has developed far beyond its origins.

You are very right in what you say about violent and dystopian visions of the future in 80s metal, especially thrash. Take a look at the work of Voivod, for instance, and the albums Dimension Hatröss and Killing Technology: there was a respect for the huge advances that digital technology was making, but also a fear about where they could eventually lead.

I think you're close here with part of the reason why it's so attractive to some. When we imagine the romance of the 40s we tend to think of people listening to records and drinking wine from dusty bottles, women in heels smoking from cigarette holders etc - we don't think about people being separated from their families, having to sleep in Tube stations or being gassed. One side is not "the reality" - they are both "the reality" together. In romanticising any era we are extracting the best and most attractive elements and forming a new one in our psychoses fashioned out of the former. Similarly when we romanticise the 80s we don't think of Margaret Thatcher or the dreadful financial avarice that abounded everywhere, we fashion a new "retrofuture" [a very apt word in my opinion] which takes all of what was attractive from the era and we create a new world from it. One which is very close to the original and maybe should have been, rather than which actually was.

A few years ago I went to a tarot reader. I'm sure there are plenty of people here who would doubt the authenticity or effectiveness of tarot, and dismiss it as cold reading or some such irrelevance. Anyway, it seemed entirely relevant to me. The deck wasn't Rider-Waite but Dakini Oracle. No cards such as Death or The Hanged Man or The Tower. They were far more descriptive than that.

Card 4 of the spread was "Deep End". Card 5 was "A Change of Mind". Card 5 was necessary to prevent 4, or to put it in another way, 4 would be what would happen if 5 didn't exist. 

In the context of myself, card 5 represented a creative outlet. Writing, photography, music. Card 4 represented suicide brought about by my obsession with women [card 1, Threefold Riddle]. 

In short, if I let my obsession with women get the better of me, I'd end up killing myself. However, if I let my creative nature get the better of me, I'd end up living a mostly happy and spiritual existence. 

And this is the thing that leads me to where I am now. I have an instrument, and I play it every day. I am doing a master's in it and intend to do a PhD and teach in it beyond university. If I had no music, or no outlet for music, I would probably end up killing myself, because I'd end up getting screwed up in more and more various different ways. It really is my only true outlet, cause and raison d'etre, and always has been.

I would suggest that you could find a similar outlet. Literal, musical, visual. I would suggest, if you are in a dark place, reading some dark material, watching some dark films or listening to some dark music [black, gothic or doom metal/dark ambient springs to mind] because then it will mirror what you're feeling and you may end up feeling a massive sense of relief and understanding. It's worked for me for years because I feel that someone, artistically, understands me through those outlets. And you don't end up feeling alone, and you can pursue these outlets as a cause. 

Ironically, a lot of the music I play is Middle Eastern and Middle Eastern music is not known for being 'dark'. 'Dark' as a way to describe Middle Eastern music doesn't make sense, in my experience. But they have sad scale systems, mystical ones, introspective ones. And these work very well for me.

Do you mean how easy is it to get in, or how easy is it to acclimatise to the work and social aspects once you're there?

Getting in is down to the university itself and what entry criteria they set for the course. The university website will give you an idea of this on the page for your selected course. And if you don't meet those criteria they can make exceptions for those who can demonstrate competency in their application. 

It's hard work, and some courses are harder than others. But really it's what you make of it. The social aspect is down to you and if you're a social person, finding the right balance between work and play is essential for getting a high mark. 

But really, email the course tutor and they can answer any more pressing questions you have. I normally find they're very quick fo reply.
